samples.summary: CLI login callback accepts any `code` delivered to its loopback port — the state/nonce binding was removed, re-opening OAuth authorization-code injection (RFC 8252 §8.9)
samples.evidence:
`startCallbackServer()` (packages/cli/src/commands/login.ts:168-227) now takes no expected nonce and resolves the login promise with whatever `?code=` first arrives at `http://127.0.0.1:/callback` (line 177-182, resolve at line 225). There is no `state` check, no Origin/Host check, and the listener is reachable by any page in the user's browser (a cross-origin navigation/``/`fetch(no-cors)` to loopback still delivers the request; the response body is unreadable but the CLI has already consumed the code). Attack: attacker runs their own `GET /auth/github?mode=cli&port=` flow, captures a valid 60s single-use code minted for THEIR account, then has the victim's browser hit `http://127.0.0.1:

/callback?code=` for a spray of ephemeral ports while `wafflebase login` is waiting. The CLI exchanges it at `POST /auth/cli/exchange` (line 56) — which requires no other proof — and silently persists the attacker's session in `~/.wafflebase/session.json`; every subsequent `upload`/`docs create` writes the victim's data into the attacker's workspace. This delta deletes the exact mitigation (nonce mint, `state` echo, constant-time compare) plus its regression test `packages/cli/test/login-callback.test.ts`, so nothing in CI will notice.

samples.summary: Backend no longer echoes a per-flow value back to the CLI callback, so the CLI cannot bind the redeemed code to the flow it started
samples.evidence: The CLI redirect is now `http://127.0.0.1:${port}/callback?code=...` with no `state` (auth.controller.ts:127-129), and `CliAuthStore.createState()`/`consumeState()` dropped the `nonce` field entirely (cli-auth.store.ts:21-47). Combined with the CLI side (login.ts:177), the loopback authorization code is delivered with zero binding to the requesting process: any code, from any user's flow, is redeemable by any listener on that port. Restoring the echo (or adding PKCE `code_challenge`/`code_verifier` on `POST /auth/cli/exchange`) is what makes the code non-injectable. Note also that `mode=cli&port=` is fully attacker-controllable from any web page, so an attacker can freely mint codes aimed at a guessed victim port.

verdict.reason: The CLI loopback callback has no per-flow binding anywhere in the chain. login.ts:36 opens the OAuth URL with only mode/port (no nonce/state sent), and the callback handler (login.ts:168-227) accepts any request to /callback, reads only `code` (line 177), and resolves the login promise with it (line 225) — no state check, no Origin/Sec-Fetch/Host check, no constant-time compare, no method restriction. Searching for the mitigation elsewhere: the backend's state token covers only the GitHub leg (github-auth.guard.ts:21-26) and its `csrf` value is never delivered to the CLI; the loopback redirect carries only `code` (auth.controller.ts:127-129); `cliExchange` (auth.controller.ts:149-153) and `CliAuthStore.consumeCode` (cli-auth.store.ts:56-64) require no port/client/flow proof, so the 60s code is pure bearer. A repo-wide grep for csrf|nonce|timingSafeEqual|state= found no CLI-side binding (only the GitHub-leg store and an unrelated HMAC guard), and docs/design/cli.md:170-198 documents this same unbound design. Attacker mints a code in their own mode=cli flow, then drives the victim's browser (or any local process) to 127.0.0.1:<port>/callback?code=<attacker-code> during the 30s window; the CLI exchanges it and persists the attacker's session (login.ts:56-60,138), so later uploads write victim data into the attacker's workspace. In-lane (auth/crypto: missing binding, accepting an unauthenticated credential) and blocking. I could not verify the historical "mitigation was removed"/deleted-test claim (no git access), but the vulnerability is present in the current tree, which is what the rubric asks.

Restoring the echo (or adding PKCE `code_challenge`/`code_verifier` on `POST /auth/cli/exchange`) is what makes the code non-injectable. verdict.reason: The code is present exactly as described. auth.controller.ts:127-129 redirects to the CLI loopback with only `code` and no per-flow value; the `csrf` minted in cli-auth.store.ts:25-34 is never returned to the CLI or echoed on the callback (grep shows `csrf` referenced only in cli-auth.store.ts and its spec), and cli-auth.store.ts:49-64 stores no flow/verifier binding for codes. The CLI loopback (login.ts:168-182, 223-226) resolves on any `GET /callback?code=...` with no state or Origin check, and POST /auth/cli/exchange (auth.controller.ts:146-162, CliExchangeDto) takes a bare code with no PKCE code_verifier. Since any web page can start a CLI flow via `GET /auth/github?mode=cli&port=<chosen>` (github-auth.guard.ts:16-30), an attacker can mint a code for their own account and inject it into a victim's open loopback listener, making the victim's CLI persist the attacker's tokens (session fixation / auth-code injection). Real, unguarded, and in the Security lane (auth binding) — blocking.

finding.summary: The new CLI login `nonce` is a bearer-grade binding secret carried in a URL query string that the request logger records verbatim (redaction covers headers only)
finding.evidence: `packages/cli/src/commands/login.ts:46` sends the secret as a query param: `${server}/auth/github?mode=cli&port=${port}&nonce=${encodeURIComponent(nonce)}`. On the backend, pino-http's request serializer logs `url: req.url` (`app.module.ts:68`) — the full path *with* query string — and the `redact.paths` list (`app.module.ts:76-83`) only censors `req.headers.authorization`, `req.headers.cookie` and `res.headers["set-cookie"]`; nothing strips query parameters. `customLogLevel` maps this 302 GET to `debug`, so it is silent at default `info`, but any deployment with `LOG_LEVEL=debug`, any 4xx on that route (→ `warn`, logged at info), or any reverse proxy / CDN access log in front of the backend captures the nonce together with the callback port, both in the same line. Attack: read one log line, then from any page in the victim's browser navigate to `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/callback?code=<attacker-code>&state=<leaked-nonce>` inside the 30s window (`login.ts:257-265`) — `nonceMatches` at `login.ts:206` passes and the CLI redeems the attacker's code, which is precisely the RFC 8252 §8.9 outcome the change claims to prevent. The whole mitigation collapses to the secrecy of a query parameter that the repo logs unredacted.

verdict.reason: The finding's core premise — a CLI login `nonce` binding secret sent as a URL query parameter — does not exist in this repository. `packages/cli/src/commands/login.ts:36` builds the OAuth URL as `${server}/auth/github?mode=cli&port=${port}` with no `nonce` component. The claimed `nonceMatches` at login.ts:206 is actually CSS inside the success-page HTML template (the file is 270 lines and line 206 is `box-shadow: ...`), and the claimed "30s window at login.ts:257-265" is the `tryListen`/`srv.on('error')` retry logic. The local callback handler (login.ts:168-182) reads only the `code` search param and never inspects `state` or any nonce, so the described attack (navigating to `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/callback?code=<attacker-code>&state=<leaked-nonce>` to satisfy a nonce check) has no check to satisfy. On the backend, `packages/backend/src/auth/github-auth.guard.ts:16-30` reads only `req.query.mode` and `req.query.port` and applies a port-range bound — there is no nonce capture and no 1..128 length bound. A repo-wide case-insensitive grep for `nonce` matches only unrelated docs, the en_US spellcheck dictionary, the `get-nonce` npm package in pnpm-lock.yaml, and `.agent-review/*` reviewer artifacts; zero hits in any source file under packages/cli or packages/backend. The logging half of the claim is accurate as written (`app.module.ts:68` serializes `url: req.url`, and `app.module.ts:76-83` redacts only `req.headers.authorization`, `req.headers.cookie`, `res.headers["set-cookie"]`), but with no nonce in the query string there is no bearer-grade secret being exposed and no RFC 8252 §8.9 mitigation to collapse. The security impact described is unreachable because the code it depends on is not present.

mergedFrom.summary: `POST /auth/cli/exchange` has no proof-of-possession: the nonce now available server-side is not required to redeem the code

finding.summary: CLI auth code is still not bound to the client (no PKCE); the nonce only gates the local listener, so an intercepted code is fully redeemable
finding.evidence: The change cites RFC 8252 §8.9, whose actual prescription for the loopback-redirect code-injection problem is PKCE. What landed is a `state` echo checked only inside the CLI's own listener (`packages/cli/src/commands/login.ts:206`). The code itself remains an unbound bearer: `POST /auth/cli/exchange` (auth.controller.ts:152-168) takes `{ code }` with no authentication, no `code_verifier`, and no reference to the nonce — `consumeCode` looks up only the code (cli-auth.store.ts:71). Attack: anyone who observes the code within its 60s TTL — from the victim's browser history/URL bar (`http://127.0.0.1:<port>/callback?code=…` is a real navigation), a browser extension, a shared/kiosk machine, or an intercepting proxy — POSTs it to /auth/cli/exchange and receives the victim's `accessToken` + `refreshToken`. The nonce does nothing here because the CLI listener is not in the path. Grepped the whole repo for pkce/code_verifier/code_challenge: zero hits. Severity is 'major' rather than 'critical' because it needs code interception, and confidence is low because I could not demonstrate a concrete interception channel in this codebase.

verdict.reason: Traced the full CLI OAuth chain independently: the CLI posts only `{ code }` (login.ts:59) with no verifier; the listener checks nothing but the presence of `code` (login.ts:177) — there is no state echo at all, contrary to the reviewer's quote; the backend mints the code from `createCode(user.id)` and delivers it in the loopback URL (auth.controller.ts:126-129); `CliExchangeDto` has only `code` (auth.dto.ts:3-7); `POST /auth/cli/exchange` is unguarded and resolves via `consumeCode(body.code)` which keys on the code alone (cli-auth.store.ts:56-64). The `csrf` value generated in `createState` (cli-auth.store.ts:25) is never sent to the CLI nor validated — it is dead. Repo-wide greps for pkce/code_verifier/code_challenge/verifier/challenge/nonce/csrf and for every call site of createState/consumeState/createCode/consumeCode/cli-exchange surface no alternate binding mechanism, no second exchange endpoint, and no device-code path. The absence claim is therefore accurate, and it is blocking under the crypto/auth lane: any party who observes the code within its 60s TTL (browser history of the real 127.0.0.1 navigation, extension, shared machine, proxy) can redeem it unauthenticated for the victim's access+refresh tokens. TTL/single-use/throttling mitigate but none binds the code to the requesting client. Severity 'major' is appropriate since exploitation needs an interception channel.
